definition: Contrite means penitent, eager to be forgiven.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word contrite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know contrite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Contrite after forgetting the anniversary, Malik cooked her favorite dinner and admitted he had no excuse worth offering.
Sheepish is much milder than contrite — an embarrassed grin over a small blunder, gone within the minute.
Apologetic is weaker than contrite — an apologetic person says the right words, while a contrite one genuinely aches to be forgiven.

Remorseful means feeling deep sorrow and guilt for a wrong you have done. Contrite holds that same sorrow and adds a reaching outward — an eagerness to be forgiven and to repair the damage now. Remorse can sit silently for years; a contrite person is already apologizing.

Shamefaced means visibly embarrassed by what you did — the flush, the lowered eyes, the wish to disappear. It stops at the look, while contrite goes to the heart: real ache over the wrong and eagerness to be forgiven. A shamefaced child hangs back; a contrite one steps forward.

The batter whose foul ball shattered the bakery window came back that evening contrite: he apologized to the owner face to face, paid for the glass out of his allowance, and swept up every splinter himself.

Contrite goes beyond 'sorry.' A sorry person may just want the moment over; a contrite one genuinely aches over the wrong and wants to be forgiven — the word's root picture is of a heart ground down by what it did.
Contrite is for visible, heartfelt remorse that seeks forgiveness right now — the contrite note, the contrite apology at the door.
Its unit-mate penitent runs deeper and longer: a penitent person turns sorrow into amends over time, often with a religious echo.
If the sorrow is a moment, call it contrite; if it is a path, call it penitent.

The bakery's new manager, Priya, mixed up the delivery list on her second Saturday, and four birthday cakes went to the wrong houses.
She could have blamed the software.
Instead she taped the list to the counter, called each family herself, and asked what would make it right.
By Monday she had driven replacement cakes across town and pinned a handwritten apology beside the register where every customer could read it.
Her boss said later that what struck him was not the mistake but how contrite she was — she seemed almost impatient to be forgiven.
One of the four families framed the apology note.
The other three became regulars, which Priya said was more than she deserved.
